questions.q: In this lab, what has to happen before any specific technology or control is chosen for Meridian's architecture?
options: A vendor proof-of-concept must be scheduled
A penetration test must be run against the current environment
A Business Attributes Profile must be built with Meridian's actual business drivers
The CISO must approve a fixed security budget
questions.explain: SABSA's discipline starts with the Business Attributes Profile -- the stakeholder-agreed list of business needs every later decision has to trace back to.

questions.q: Why is the cardholder-data environment (CDE) placed on its own isolated VLAN rather than left on the general corporate network?
options: It makes the network diagram easier to draw
VLANs are required for SOC 2 regardless of what they contain
It removes the need for any access control on the segment
It shrinks PCI DSS audit scope to the isolated segment instead of the entire corporate network
questions.explain: Network segmentation is what lets Meridian defend a small, auditable boundary instead of treating every system that could reach cardholder data as in-scope.

questions.q: What does tokenizing cardholder data at intake accomplish for Meridian, according to the business-alignment case made in this lab?
options: It eliminates the need for any encryption elsewhere in the system
It replaces the need for a Business Attributes Profile entirely
It shrinks the CDE boundary, which reduces both audit cost (Regulatory standing) and ongoing security spend (Cost discipline) at once
It satisfies only the Operational resilience attribute and no others
questions.explain: Tokenization is highlighted precisely because it serves two named business attributes simultaneously, which is why it's prioritized over a point solution that satisfies only one.

questions.q: What distinguishes the architect's job in this lab from the engineer's job described back in Lesson 1?
options: The architect decides which controls the business needs and why, tracing each one back to a named business attribute
The architect writes the actual firewall rules and IAM policies
The architect's work has nothing to do with the engineering team's implementation
There is no real difference once a framework like SABSA is involved
questions.explain: Lesson 1 drew this exact line: an engineer builds and operates a control; an architect decides which controls are needed and justifies that decision in business terms.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the one-page architecture decision record produced at the end of this lab?
options: To replace the need for a formal GRC program
To document the decision, its business driver, the alternative considered, and why that alternative was rejected
To serve only as an internal engineering changelog with no business content
To satisfy a PCI DSS requirement that mandates this exact document format
questions.explain: The decision record captures a traceable line from a design choice back to a Business Attributes Profile driver and the rejected alternative -- exactly the artifact a real architecture review produces.
